title: NP-intermediate \(\omega\)-categorical CSPs
formal:
Assume \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\). Does there exist a countable \(\omega\)-categorical relational structure \(\Gamma\) in a finite relational signature such that its fixed-template constraint satisfaction problem is NP-intermediate? Explicitly, the required three conditions are
\[\operatorname{CSP}(\Gamma)\in\mathrm{NP},\qquad\operatorname{CSP}(\Gamma)\notin\mathrm P,\qquad\operatorname{CSP}(\Gamma)\text{ is not NP-complete}.\]
Completeness uses deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions, as in the source’s hardness constructions. No effective presentation or uniform construction of the infinite template is required.
why: This asks whether the principal symmetry condition for infinite-domain CSP algebra allows intermediate NP complexity at all. An example would locate a precise limit of tractability-versus-completeness classifications; a negative answer would establish a much broader NP dichotomy than the currently conjectured finitely bounded homogeneous framework.
status_note: Question 3 of the checked MFCS 2026 publication explicitly restates the conditional NP-intermediate existence question. The April 2026 preprint version history and bounded later primary-source searches were checked on 16 September 2026; no matching solution was found. The new polynomial-hierarchy completeness results and the older coNP-intermediate construction do not resolve it. This is a dated, bounded status review, not exhaustive certification of present openness.

importance.reason: Determines whether omega-categoricity alone permits intermediate NP complexity, testing the reach of the main algebraic framework beyond currently conjectured infinite-template dichotomy classes.
importance.basis: Individual reading of MFCS 2026 Question 3, the older coNP-intermediate construction, and the monograph’s exact NP-versus-coNP distinction.

sentences: Assuming P differs from NP, the question asks whether an omega-categorical fixed-template CSP can have intermediate NP complexity.
Omega-categoricity means finitely many symmetry orbits at each fixed tuple length, and the template has a finite relational signature.
The CSP must lie in NP while being neither polynomial-time decidable nor NP-complete under polynomial-time many-one reductions.
CoNP-intermediate examples and completeness at every polynomial-hierarchy level are known, but they do not supply the required NP-intermediate example.
A resolution would determine whether this broad symmetry condition alone rules out intermediate complexity inside NP.

definitions:
A finite relational signature \(\tau\) is a finite list of relation symbols with fixed positive integer arities. A template \(\Gamma\) has a nonempty finite or countably infinite domain and a relation \(R^\Gamma\subseteq\Gamma^r\) for every \(r\)-ary symbol. A homomorphism \(h:I\to\Gamma\) preserves all positive relation tuples: if \((i_1,\ldots,i_r)\in R^I\), then \((h(i_1),\ldots,h(i_r))\in R^\Gamma\). It need not be injective or preserve missing tuples.

An automorphism is a domain bijection preserving both membership and nonmembership in every relation. It acts on ordered \(k\)-tuples coordinate by coordinate. The structure is \(\omega\)-categorical when, for each fixed positive integer \(k\), this action has finitely many orbits on \(\Gamma^k\). For a countably infinite finite-signature structure, this is equivalent to its complete first-order theory having exactly one countably infinite model up to isomorphism. Finite templates satisfy the orbit convention too. The number of orbits may depend on \(k\), and no procedure computing them is assumed.

The language \(\operatorname{CSP}(\Gamma)\) accepts encodings of finite \(\tau\)-structures \(I\) exactly when there is a homomorphism \(I\to\Gamma\). Encode the instance domain \([n]\) by unary \(n\), then in signature order the explicitly listed relation tuples, each list preceded by a unary length and with binary indices separated by delimiters. This polynomial encoding counts isolated elements; repeated coordinates and duplicate tuples are allowed. The empty domain maps by the empty function. Malformed inputs are rejected. Let \(L\) be the full bit length. The signature and template are fixed before instances arrive and are not supplied as an infinite table or an oracle.

A language is in \(\mathrm P\) when some deterministic multitape Turing machine decides it on every bit string in at most \(C(L+1)^d\) bit steps for fixed positive integers \(C,d\). A language is in \(\mathrm{NP}\) when membership has a certificate of polynomially bounded length checked by a deterministic polynomial-time verifier. No randomness or advice is used. Importantly, a certificate for this infinite-template CSP need not list actual domain elements of \(\Gamma\); it can use any finite encoding and verifier proving the same language is in NP. Omega-categoricity alone does not guarantee NP membership.

A polynomial-time many-one reduction from a language \(K\) to a language \(Q\) is a total polynomial-time computable function \(r\) on binary strings such that \(x\in K\) if and only if \(r(x)\in Q\). A language \(Q\) is NP-complete if it is in NP and every NP language reduces to it in this sense. These reductions make one target instance and do not make adaptive oracle queries. A language is NP-intermediate if it lies in NP but satisfies neither tractability nor completeness. The constants and programs in these class definitions can depend on the fixed language or reduction; no common exponent for all templates is intended.

The question is existence of a mathematical template with all the stated properties, not a metaproblem receiving descriptions of arbitrary infinite structures. No finite list of forbidden patterns, homogeneous expansion, finite domain or algorithm deciding the relations of \(\Gamma\) is imposed. For context, coNP is the class of complements of NP languages; coNP-intermediate means in coNP but neither in P nor coNP-complete under the same reduction convention.
answer_criterion: Under the hypothesis \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\), give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean either that such a template exists or that none exists. A positive proof must establish omega-categoricity, a finite relational signature, NP membership, absence of a deterministic polynomial-time decision algorithm, and absence of polynomial-time many-one NP completeness. An abstract NP-intermediate language or an unrestricted infinite template without omega-categoricity is insufficient. A negative proof must show, under the hypothesis, that every permitted template whose CSP lies in NP has a CSP in P or is NP-complete. CoNP intermediacy, completeness at a higher complexity level, or a dichotomy only for a narrower subclass does not settle this question.

source_formulation.text: Assuming P differs from NP, is there an NP-intermediate CSP with an omega-categorical template?
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of Question 3, which restates Bodirsky’s Question 49; NP completeness uses the source’s polynomial-time many-one convention.

context_blocks.text: Ladner’s theorem gives NP-intermediate languages if P differs from NP, but it does not automatically place them inside every structured family of computational problems. The issue here is whether an intermediate NP language can be realized as a fixed CSP while retaining finitely many symmetry types at every tuple length.

Finite-template CSPs satisfy the P versus NP-complete dichotomy, so a finite template cannot witness the desired intermediate behavior under the hypothesis. Allowing an infinite domain admits new CSP languages, while omega-categoricity retains the symmetry property supporting many algebraic methods.

Bodirsky and Grohe already construct omega-categorical CSPs in coNP that are neither tractable nor coNP-complete, assuming P differs from coNP. Their construction adapts Ladner’s diagonalization by choosing a suitable infinite family of forbidden tournaments. This demonstrates intermediate complexity on the complementary side, but does not provide NP membership for the required example.

Taking the complement of a coNP-intermediate language produces an NP-intermediate language, but complementing a CSP language need not produce another CSP language. Every CSP is closed under inverse homomorphisms and disjoint unions of finite instances. Such closure properties constrain representation and do not automatically survive complementation.

The 2026 paper constructs omega-categorical CSPs complete for every level of the polynomial hierarchy, the decision classes described by a fixed number of alternating existential and universal blocks of polynomial-length certificates. Its constructions extend the known complementary-side examples, yet Question 3 explicitly retains NP intermediacy as a separate problem.

The Bodirsky–Pinsker dichotomy concerns the narrower class of first-order reducts of finitely bounded homogeneous structures. In that setting a homogeneous structure has all finite induced partial isomorphisms extend to automorphisms, finite boundedness specifies its finite induced substructures by finitely many forbidden patterns, and a first-order reduct retains finitely many parameter-free definable relations. None of these restrictions is imposed here; a dichotomy for that subclass would not rule out an intermediate template elsewhere.
